articles.title_zh: Online claims revive mercury mystery around tomb of first Chinese emperor
articles.content_orig:
A Weibo hashtag about ancient cinnabar sites has reignited debate over the ‘rivers and seas’ in Qin Shi Huang’s mausoleum
Online claims that archaeologists have identified the source of mercury in the mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang – China’s first emperor, who unified the country more than 2,000 years ago – have revived interest in ancient cinnabar sites in northwestern China’s Shaanxi province.
The claims, which sent related hashtags trending on social media late last month, centred on three sites in Xunyang where archaeologists last year found evidence of cinnabar mining, processing and transport during the pre-Qin and Qin-Han periods.

articles.title_orig: Tennessee Inmate in Critical Condition After ‘Torturous’ Botched Execution, Lawyer Says
articles.title_zh: Tennessee Inmate in Critical Condition After ‘Torturous’ Botched Execution, Lawyer Says
articles.content_orig:
What we know about Christa Pikeâs condition after failed execution
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike is in "critical condition, receiving life-saving care" at hospital, after surviving two lethal injection attempts, leading the state's governor to halt all executions for the year.
"We don't have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment," her lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters on Thursday. "But we do know that she is alive right now."
Her lawyers are now asking for her sentence to be commuted. Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.
She was injected with two lethal doses of pentobarbital on Wednesday but remained alive, her lawyers said. She was then sent to hospital in an ambulance.
Watch: Witnesses recount Christa Pike's failed execution attempt
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer.
Her attempted execution on Wednesday was the subject of a last-minute legal battle. This culminated in the US Supreme Court allowing the lethal injections to go ahead.
Slemmer's mother May Martinez, who was among those who wanted the execution to take place and who travelled to Tennessee to witness it, told NBC News after the botched attempt that "it was a mess".
On Thursday afternoon, Pike's lawyers offered more details about what happened during the attempted execution, describing a harrowing scene shrouded in secrecy.
"Last night, the execution team attempted to establish an IV line for an hour," Spivey said. "I counted at least seven needles used in her left arm alone, one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm after an unsuccessful attempt."
Spivey said that observers were kept in a dark room behind a closed curtain, after the second lethal dose had been administered and "it was clear that Miss Pike was still breathing" minutes later.
"No-one knew what was going on behind that curtain," Spivey said. "I had no idea when and if medical professionals began to assist."
Spivey said the state's governor must commute Christa's sentence now,  a request that was denied previously.
Stephen Ferrell, another of Pike's lawyers, said they were also looking at other legal options.
"We want to think this through and we want to make sure that Christa recovers and has some input in what she wants," he said.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered an independent review and said on Thursday the investigation into Pike's botched execution "will be thorough", adding that "it's going to take time".
"There are a lot of questions," Lee said. "The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered, and that's what this investigation is for."
Lee has not made clear who will conduct the independent review of the state's execution procedures.
His order to pause all executions will overlap with the planned 3 December execution of convicted murderer Gary Sutton.
The Tennessee Department of Correction, which handled the execution, issued a statement defending its handling of the case.
It said in a statement that it "followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general's office".
"The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening."
Pike was given two doses of the chemical pentobarbital, in accordance with state protocol when the first attempt fails, but was still alive afterwards, according to court filings by her lawyers.
"This execution is causing Ms Pike unnecessary agony and occurring in violation of his right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment," her lawyers said.
The Tennessee attorney general's office said in a statement that it agreed with the decision to call for an investigation, adding: "We need to know what happened."
US Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn, who is running for Tennessee governor, described the situation as "tragic".
"While there should be a thorough review of what happened and why the process failed, the answer is simple: bring back the electric chair," Blackburn said.
Democrat Jerri Green, Blackburn's opponent, criticised her for wanting to "bring back one of the most cruel forms of capital punishment".
"As governor, I would put a moratorium on all future executions," Green said on X.
This is the second time in 2026 Tennessee officials attempted and failed to execute a prisoner.
In May, the execution of Tony Carruthers was called off after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal drug. Carruthers was given a year's reprieve.

articles.title_orig: Israel's Netanyahu: Co-pilot of flydubai plane underwent radical Islamist indoctrination
articles.title_zh: Israel's Netanyahu: Co-pilot of flydubai plane underwent radical Islamist indoctrination
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".
The Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two hours into its journey on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control to land safely.
Netanyahu told Fox News that it was looking "very likely" that the attacker, who he said was an Omani national, "was going to down the plane".
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) state news agency reports investigations have begun there to determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose".
The Interior Ministry of Saudi Arabia - where the plane made an emergency landing - said that both the pilot and co-pilot had been sent back to the UAE on Thursday morning after medical teams had cleared them.
UAE officials earlier claimed jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft on which the attack took place is registered there and flies under its flag.
Netanyahu told Fox that once the attacker had been subdued and tied up by passengers and crew, he was "calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal - that's not a question".
Passenger Almog Itali said it felt like a "rollercoaster" as Flight FZ1073 fell 17,000ft in less than two minutes
"And with all the passengers in there, and if you couple that with what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that were found in his background, I think... that'll give us a pretty good clue."
However, he stressed that he did not want to draw any firm conclusions as to motive yet.
Both US President Donald Trump and UAE officials have indicated to the media that Iran may be responsible for the incident, without definitively blaming Tehran.
Trump told reporters on Thursday that Iran would be "hit very hard" if it was deemed to have been involved in the attack.
Pilots from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel were usually not allowed to fly there, Netanyahu said when asked about how the suspected Omani pilot came to be on the plane.
He added: "Obviously there was a loophole here and we're taking care of that among other things... with the full co-operation, I have to say, of the Emirati government, so we're both interested in making sure this doesn't happen again."
Oman has not formally established official ties with Israel , unlike the UAE.
The prime minister was also asked earlier on the same network whether there was an indication if Iran was involved, he replied: "It's too early to say".
Flydubai passenger describes hugging his children as plane nosedived during attack
Who is the 'hero' Indian pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight?
Both Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the stabbed pilot, Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar was a "hero".
India's ambassador to the UAE Deepak Mittal visited Captain Machhar in hospital on Thursday, the Indian Mission confirmed on social media, stating he was "in good health and recovering well".
The Indian government has praised Smit Machchhar for his "immense courage"
Preliminary findings from a separate Israeli investigation into the incident, suggest that the alleged attacker intended to crash the plane, an Israeli security source told BBC Arabic.
The source said the investigation - led by Israel's intelligence agency Mossad - interviewed passengers after they arrived in Tel Aviv to establish what had happened on the plane.
Flydubai's flight FZ1073, with more than 170 people on board, took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben Gurion Airport.
Two hours later, the 17,000ft drop in altitude was reported on the plane tracking website Flightradar24 and minutes later the plane signalled an emergency code.
At about 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent, landing safely at  Tabuk Airport in the north west of Saudi.
Flydubai has since suspended flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv as it carried out its own investigation into the incident.
Israel's Transportation Ministry said the suspension aligns with Netanyahu's directive.
Israeli airlines including El Al, Israir and Arkia said plans were in place to operate rescue flights from Dubai starting on Friday to bring back stranded passengers.
The Transportation Ministry also said it sent an urgent request to Etihad Airlines to increase the number of flights between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv.

articles.title_orig: FBI arrests Massachusetts man on charge of stalking conservative podcaster Katie Miller
articles.title_zh: FBI arrests Massachusetts man on charge of stalking conservative podcaster Katie Miller
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: New York AG Letitia James will take over investigation of alleged rape at Cornell, Gov. Kathy Hochul says
The FBI on Thursday arrested a man on a charge of stalking former Trump administration adviser Katie Miller, an administration official familiar with the investigation told NBC News.
John Anthony Proia III, 41, was arrested and charged with stalking over allegations that he called, texted and left voicemails with “disturbing messages” about the victim, who was described as a former political adviser, and her husband, who is currently a high-level federal government employee, the Justice Department said in a news release.
The Justice Department did not name Katie Miller, though an administration official familiar with the investigation confirmed to NBC News that the victim is Miller, who is married to White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller and hosts a popular conservative podcast.
“Thank you Todd Blanche, Leah Foley, and the FBI Washington Field Office for keeping me and my family safe. Good to see a Boston grand jury indict this man,” Miller wrote in a post on X on Thursday, referring to Attorney General Todd Blanche and U.S. Attorney Leah Foley.
Proia was indicted by a federal grand jury in Boston on Thursday on one count of cyberstalking after being arrested earlier in the day. He allegedly contacted the former political adviser more than 40 times over the course of less than two months, according to the Justice Department.
The defendant also allegedly sent disturbing messages to Miller’s parents during the August 2026 to September 2026 time frame cited in court documents.
“As alleged in the Indictment, the defendant repeatedly and relentlessly targeted the victim, her husband and her family with deeply disturbing communications that profoundly disrupted their lives,” Foley said in a statement.
Ted Docks, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Boston Division, wrote in a statement on Thursday that Proia was arrested “for allegedly engaging in a sustained campaign of harassment to frighten this victim and her family, inflicting significant emotional distress.”
Proia made the calls, sent text messages and left voicemails from “an ever-changing series of unfamiliar phone numbers” to Miller, who lives in the Washington, D.C., area, the DOJ said.
The department added that those phone numbers were obtained through applications that provide free phone numbers for calling and messaging via Voice over Internet Protocol. The applications allow a user to hide their identity and easily generate new phone numbers, according to court filings.
According to court documents, Miller sometimes received multiple communications from Proia in one day, including calls made late at night. Miller did answer some of the calls, but Proia also left voicemails, the DOJ said.
The calls “were allegedly made by what appeared to be a male caller employing a menacing tone and often using expletives,” the Justice Department said.
The Justice Department also detailed some text messages sent to phone numbers associated with Miller’s parents.
In one message, Proia allegedly wrote to Miller’s mother, calling Stephen Miller “evil” and Katie Miller a “creature.” Another message allegedly featured a photo of Katie Miller, while another read, “My god, how can you be proud of this filth?”
In a text message to the victim’s father, Proia allegedly wrote, “Hey [first name of victim’s father], how goes it? Hope your daughter marrying a Jewish Nazi/white supremacist is working out for you and [first name of victim’s mother]. Did you raise her to be trash or did that just happen naturally?”
Proia’s arrest comes after Bloomberg reported over the weekend that two senior FBI officials in Washington were demoted and reassigned to FBI headquarters due to concerns that the agency was not moving efficiently enough to investigate threatening phone calls made to Miller, three people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg.
Darren Cox, the agency’s Washington Field Office’s assistant director in charge, said in a statement to Bloomberg that the move was a personnel decision made at the field office level based on “our constant evaluation of mission needs.”
Michael Kosnar is the Justice Department Producer for NBC News.
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.

By CHRISTINE RENDÓN, US SENIOR REPORTER and DIANA COOPER, US SENIOR SHOWBIZ REPORTER
Published: 18:08 EDT, 1 October 2026 | Updated: 21:11 EDT, 1 October 2026
Halle Berry 's ex Olivier Martinez has been granted temporary primary custody of their 12-year-old son Maceo after accusing the actress of physically abusing him - claims Berry has slammed as 'entirely meritless.'
In bombshell court documents filed in Los Angeles on Thursday and obtained by The Daily Mail, Martinez alleged Berry 'physically abused our son by jumping on him and choking him' during a September 26, 2026 incident.
Martinez was granted a temporary domestic violence restraining order against Berry, which protects both himself and their son from the actress. The order requires Berry to stay 100 yards away from Martinez.
The Monster's Ball actress has also lost 50/50 custody, and will be allowed to see their son only during court-ordered visitation two days a week and every other weekend until a hearing on October 16.
Berry's attorney Marina Beck told the Daily Mail the filing is 'entirely meritless' and claimed that Martinez is 'an individual with a well-documented history of erratic, possessive and violent behavior.'
She added that Berry is 'used to this kind of outrageous conduct' from Martinez and 'deeply saddened' by the situation, though she will 'not allow it to deter her from fighting for Maceo’s best interests and providing him with the love and support he needs.'
The filing lays bare a series of alleged disputes between Berry, Martinez, and their son over the last few years - with the most recent one prompting him to take legal action against her.

'Throughout the last year-and-a-half, Ms. Berry has wrestled Maceo to the ground and forced him to "tap out,"' Martinez alleged.
The documents allege Berry has 'grabbed our son's neck from the back when he is not looking and forced him to tap out' multiple times previously - instances that she allegedly insisted were done in jest, but which their son disliked.
In her full statement, Berry's attorney told the Daily Mail: 'To say this filing is entirely meritless and deliberately misleading would be an understatement.'
'There is voluminous evidence, including numerous judicial rulings, that Olivier Martinez repeatedly violated court orders and interfered with necessary therapeutic and educational interventions to the detriment of his and Halle Berry's minor son Maceo - misconduct for which Mr. Martinez has already been legally sanctioned.'
'In a way, today's filing is not entirely unexpected from an individual with a well-documented history of erratic, possessive and violent behavior. Fortunately, Halle is used to this kind of outrageous conduct from Mr. Martinez and, while she is deeply saddened, she will not allow it to deter her from fighting for Maceo’s best interests and providing him with the love and support he needs.'
Berry and Martinez have also been ordered to participate in confidential mediation to discuss custody, according to legal documents obtained by TMZ .
The incident which triggered the restraining order allegedly all began after Berry told Maceo he looked 'so stupid' and was 'an idiot' while playing a virtual reality game and wearing specialized goggles.
According to Martinez, Maceo told him his mother 'came into Maceo's bedroom and began pushing Maceo. From what I can tell, the initial contact appeared to be intended to be in a joking manner. Maceo told Petitioner [Berry], "Stop. Let me finish the game first." This sent Petitioner into a rage.'
The actor further alleged in the court document: 'Petitioner told Maceo that he looks "so stupid" and is "such an idiot' for playing this game with the VR goggle.
'The situation escalated from there. Petitioner jumped on Maceo and started physically fighting with him. She grabbed Maceo by the neck and started choking him while shouting, "Who is dominant now?! Who is dominant?"'
'Maceo told me he had to fight back,' Martinez wrote in the filing. 'Through his efforts, he managed to escape Petitioner's grip. He started screaming, at which point, Petitioner's boyfriend came into the room.
According to Martinez, Maceo claimed that Berry's fiance, Van Hunt, treated him 'fair.'
The document states that Hunt 'defended Maceo as he was packing his clothes to leave when Petitioner tried to tell him that he could not take his clothes because Petitioner had bought them for him.'
'Throughout the last year-and-a-half, Ms. Berry has wrestled Maceo to the ground and forced him to "tap out,"' Martinez alleged
'When Maceo said that the clothes had been given to him so he could take them with him, Petitioner's boyfriend agreed with him and convinced Petitioner to allow him to pack his clothes.'
Martinez claimed that on the night of the alleged incident, he received a 'frantic call' from his son asking him to pick him up '"right now."'
Martinez then contacted Berry over text message about picking Maceo up, asking if she was 'OK with it.'
Text messages included in the filing show the correspondence between Martinez and Berry, with the actress allegedly responding to Martinez's pick up request: 'No I'm not ok with it. He wants to fight his mother?? What kind of kid are we raising."'
Martinez alleged he had several more calls with his son and could hear Berry's voice in one of the conversations. He claims to have heard his son telling Berry that he is going to 'leave forever', with Berry 'yelling' to their son, 'Good. Good. I don't want to see anymore.'
He alleges to have received several more urgent-sounding text messages from Maceo asking when he will arrive.
When he arrived to the house, Maceo emerged with Hunt, who was carrying bags of Maceo's clothing and 'had a shocked look on his face' when asked by Martinez about what had happened. He alleged Hunt 'did not respond to my question.'

articles.title_orig: France school protests escalate into ‘urban violence’ as PM calls crisis cabinet meeting
articles.title_zh: France school protests escalate into ‘urban violence’ as PM calls crisis cabinet meeting
articles.content_orig:
About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents under way outside high schools around the country
A fast-growing protest by high-school students over long hours, teacher shortages and decaying facilities has escalated into “urban violence”, the French government has warned, as it said many schools would switch to online classes to protect teachers and pupils.
The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, called a crisis cabinet meeting on Thursday and told ministers to cancel travel plans to deal with the demonstrations, which erupted in the Paris region last week but have snowballed across the country.
Lecornu’s office said: “This upsurge in violence makes it virtually impossible to maintain the continuity of public education and is exposing staff and students to danger.” The education minister, Édouard Geffray, is to meet pupil representatives on Friday.
About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents were under way outside high schools around the country, police said, with more than 160 shut down as a result. Access was also blocked to about 30 university campuses on Thursday, including in Paris and Marseille.
Nearly 3,000 lycée students – aged between 15 and 18 – have been detained since the start of the protests, including 1,949 on Thursday alone, the interior ministry said. More than 300 police and dozens of firefighters, teachers and pupils have been injured.
The pupils’ grievances range from overloaded timetables and overcrowded classes to insufficient teachers and unbearable temperatures during heatwaves earlier this year. Riot police have been deployed to confront the increasingly violent protests.
Injuries have mainly been from hurled objects but also from police-fired riot-control projectiles, with the interior ministry announcing an internal police investigation after accusations of excessive force and brutality by officers against three pupils.
Rubbish bins have been set on fire outside many schools and more serious arson attempts have been reported inside some buildings. Fire damage in one school in Nantes in the north-west was so extensive that it will stay closed for a month, authorities said.
In the northern city of Caen, 16-year-old Maelle said she wished those setting bins on fire would protest “with words”. Students were protesting “against this government that doesn’t invest in heating, air conditioning, or teachers’ salaries”, she told AFP.
In Strasbourg in the north-east, tram services were temporarily suspended to “restrict the movements of rioters and demonstrators”, the regional prefect said, after protesting students obstructed the tracks with crowd control barriers.
“There are 35 of us per classroom,” one 17-year-old Strasbourg student said. “There aren’t enough toilets, and there are water leaks in some rooms. The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There’s zero budget, zero resources.”
Several bin fires were also reported in the southern city of Toulouse; while in Lille, young people wearing black hoodies destroyed a bus stop. In Marseille, there were attempts to light fires inside two schools. In one, a teacher was splashed with petrol.
While many teachers and several headteachers have reported being physically threatened and sometimes attacked, some support their pupils. Juliette Estiville, a high-school Spanish teacher in Paris, said that the police response had disgusted her.
“I’m actually here just to provide protection, to form a barrier between the police and the students,” she said. “Today went well, it’s going well, but I think that the teachers who come to the blockades are really there to protect our young people.”
The government has accused the radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party of encouraging the protests, with several LFI MPs and mayors, including Bally Bagayoko, the LFI mayor of the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis, cheered at demonstrations.
The party’s candidate for the 2027 presidential election, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, insisted on Thursday that LFI backed “non-violent methods of struggle” and added that his “greatest worry is an unbearable level of police violence against these young people”.

Sign up for the Breaking News US email
The supreme court today said it will review whether the Trump administration can enforce its policy of denying bond hearings for immigrants to determine whether they should remain detained while their cases are adjudicated.
The novel move to impose mandatory detention is another feature of Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown during his second term in office, and has now made its way to the top court after several appeals court judges ruled that the policy violated federal law and fails to provide immigrants with due process.
However, those decisions conflict with rulings by the fifth and eighth circuits – which ruled that immigrants accused of illegally entering and remaining in the US must be detained while their deportation cases are pending.
The case that will be part of the supreme court’s docket for the 2026-27 term focuses on Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha , a citizen of Brazil, who authorities say he entered the US illegally two decades ago and applied for asylum in 2016 and was granted a work permit.
He sought a bond hearing after an immigration judge determined that his detention was mandatory after his September 2025 arrest. After Barbosa da Cunha sued, a federal judge ordered that be provided a hearing or released. An immigration judge found that Barbosa da Cunha did not present a flight risk or danger to persons or property, and ordered him released on bond. The administration appealed against the decision.
The number of people in immigration detention has shot up since Trump returned to office. It was more than 65,000 in July 2026, up from about 40,000 at the end of Joe Biden’s administration.
On Thursday evening, the Department of Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin primed a crowd of Oklahoma supporters awaiting Donald Trump with a conspiracy theory: Democrats are plotting a communist takeover of the nation.
“In order for them to take us to a socialist country and move us right into a communist country, they have to create chaos… they’ve got to change the demographics,” Mullin said, referring to the presence of undocumented immigrants.
“They’ve got to usher in chaos. And then they’ll come out and say ‘Hey look this government doesn’t work. You need us to take charge.’ And that’s how you end up with a communist country.”
Mullin spoke at the rally for about 15 minutes, urging the attendees to vote for what he framed as an existential battle over the nation’s future.
A federal law, known as the Hatch Act, is supposed to bar government officials from taking part in partisan campaign events, but the law is supposed to be enforced by the US Office of Special Counsel, which is currently run by a former staffer for the Republican chair of the Senate judiciary committee.
While complaints against Trump officials have been disregarded, the office recently announced sanctions against five officials who served in the Biden administration in 2024.

According to Ana Ceballos, a Los Angeles Times correspondent who is serving as the print pool reporter on the trip, the van she was in reached 98 mph at one point during the drive.
We are still waiting for Donald Trump’s second rally speech of the day, at the Choctaw Event Center in Durant, Oklahoma.
According to a reporter traveling with the president, the event has been delayed by bad weather, which has forced Trump to drive there from his previous stop in Denton, Texas, rather than fly by helicopter.
The two locations are at least 90 minutes apart by car, so we might be waiting a while for Trump to join Mike Mazzei, the Republican candidate for Oklahoma governor who has spoken already.
The rally crowd is currently being treated to a Guns N’ Roses cover of Live and Let Die, according to a local news station’s livestream of the rally . Trump’s White House was criticized for using that song at rallies in 2020, as he downplayed the threat of the Covid-19 pandemic.
In what is shaping up to be a good midterm for Democrats in most of the US, the governor’s race in Oregon could prove to be an exception.
Republican state legislator Christine Drazan is backed by 46% of voters, according to a new poll commissioned by Oregon Public Broadcasting, as the Democratic incumbent governor Tina Kotek hovered close behind with 44%.
A Republican has not been elected to the state’s top office in over four decades.
Kotek defeated Drazan in the 2022 governor’s race, winning 47% of the vote to Drazan’s 43.5%, and making history as one of the first two openly lesbian governors elected that year, along with Maura Healey of Massachusetts.
That race, however, featured a prominent third candidate, Betsy Johnson, a conservative Democrat, who is not on the ballot this year and took 8.6% of the vote.
As OPB reports, in 2022, Drazan led most public polls through November, only to see her lead collapse in the final days of the contest.
In the current rematch, Drazan has taken Kotek to task over her inability to curb homelessness in Oregon and the recent exodus of major corporate hubs during her tenure. Meanwhile, Kotek has accused Drazan of being more loyal to Trump than to Oregonians.
Donald Trump’s remarks in Texas, weeks before the midterm elections his party is in danger of losing, have just concluded with the ritual playing of YMCA.
Trump’s speech veered very far away from a discussion of the virtues of the Republican Senate candidate he was there to praise, Ken Paxton, and devolved instead into a typical rally speech, in which the president recited a number of boasts and false claims that he has made previously.
Among other things unrelated to the Texas Senate race, Trump once again claimed that the Saudi king told him, during his visit to the kingdom in May 2025, that the United States was “dead” during the presidency of Joe Biden.
“American trucking is back. Two years ago, our country was dead. You know, this was said to me by the king, by the leader, by the crown prince of Saudi Arabia,” Trump said.
The president has made this claim, that the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, told him the US was “a dead country” before he returned and instantly made it ”the hottest country in the world”, dozens of times since he returned from Riyadh in early 2025. articles.title_orig: Lindsay Clancy lawyer’s bid to get killer mom’s murder charges tossed is slapped down
articles.title_zh: Lindsay Clancy lawyer’s bid to get killer mom’s murder charges tossed is slapped down
articles.content_orig:
A Massachusetts judge has denied Lindsay Clancy's attempt to have the murder charges against her thrown out , clearing the way for prosecutors to pursue a retrial in the high-profile case involving the deaths of her three children.
In a ruling issued Thursday, Plymouth Superior Court Judge William F. Sullivan rejected the defense's Rule 25 motion for a required finding of not guilty following September's mistrial. Under Massachusetts law, a Rule 25 motion asks a judge to determine whether prosecutors presented sufficient evidence for a reasonable jury to convict.
Clancy's attorney, Kevin Reddington, argued the Commonwealth failed to prove two key elements of its case: that Clancy killed her three children and that she was criminally responsible for her actions at the time.
Sullivan disagreed, finding that prosecutors presented enough evidence for a reasonable jury to conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that Clancy committed the killings and could be held criminally responsible.
“There was evidence introduced, both physical and circumstantial, that would permit a rational trier of fact to find beyond a reasonable doubt the elements of the charge of murder," Sullivan wrote.
The decision does not determine guilt or innocence. Rather, it means the judge found the evidence presented during the first trial was legally sufficient for the case to proceed to a new jury.
The ruling represents a victory for prosecutors, who have maintained that Clancy carefully planned the killings of her children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, on January 24, 2023, then tried to kill herself, while her husband was briefly out of the family's Duxbury home.
Newsweek has contacted Reddington by email and left a message with Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy J. Cruz's office seeking comment.
According to the decision, prosecutors introduced both physical and circumstantial evidence showing that Clancy was alone with the children during the relevant time period. Her husband, Patrick Clancy, testified that he left the house to pick up takeout food and medication and later returned to find evidence of violence inside the home before discovering his children in the basement.
Medical examiners testified that the children died from asphyxia or complications resulting from mechanical asphyxia. Prosecutors alleged the children were strangled with exercise bands.
The judge also rejected the defense's challenge to the state's evidence regarding criminal responsibility. During the trial, both sides agreed that Clancy suffered from a serious mental illness at the time. The central dispute was whether that illness rendered her legally incapable of appreciating the wrongfulness of her conduct or conforming her behavior to the law.
Sullivan noted that three prosecution experts testified that Clancy retained those capacities, even if defense experts reached different conclusions. Resolving those competing opinions, he wrote, is a matter for a jury rather than a judge.
Thursday's decision marks the second time Sullivan has rejected the defense's bid to dismiss the case, finding on both occasions that prosecutors presented sufficient evidence for a jury to consider the charges.
“For the first time, the defendant is arguing that there is no evidence she did this,” Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham told the judge during Tuesday's hearing. “I’d suggest to you the entire record is voluminous as to information supporting the fact that she did this.”
A hearing is scheduled for November 2, when the parties are expected to address several unresolved issues, including Clancy's motion to block a retrial on double jeopardy grounds and the defense's request for a court inquiry into Michael Desronvil, the holdout juror who wanted to convict Clancy.
Defense attorneys have sought scrutiny of Desronvil's phone records as part of their effort to investigate the circumstances surrounding the mistrial and the conduct of the jury's deliberations.
Paul Mauro, an attorney and Fox News contributor, wrote on X after Sullivan's ruling, "Unsurprising. He should similarly swat down the double jeopardy motion and the request to review the holdout juror's phone."
Prosecutors have not yet said whether they intend to retry Clancy. Their options include pursuing another first-degree murder case, seeking lesser charges such as second-degree murder or manslaughter, or declining to move forward altogether.
If a retrial is ordered, a new jury would once again be asked to decide whether Clancy is guilty of murdering her three children or whether her mental state at the time rendered her not criminally responsible.

articles.title_zh: Joey Porter Jr. felt "disrespected" and "underappreciated" by Steelers
articles.content_orig:
On Wednesday night, the Dallas Cowboys made a move that would at least temporarily boost their injury-decimated secondary when they traded with the Pittsburgh Steelers for cornerback Joey Porter Jr.
The Cowboys sent Pittsburgh a conditional 2027 sixth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick in exchange for Porter, who had been seeking a contract extension with the Steelers since the offseason. Per ESPN, Porter must be on the gameday roster for two contests this season for the 2027 pick to go through.
It might be seen as a risk for the Cowboys to give up a second-round pick without having a contract in place for Porter. A source with knowledge of the situation told Newsweek that Dallas made the move for Porter in a bid to win this season. Owner Jerry Jones has ambitions to win the Super Bowl with this team, and the secondary needed an immediate fix amid a 1-2 start.
The Cowboys are not concerned about signing Porter to a new deal at this point in the season and have not offered the 2023 second-round pick a contract extension.
"The Cowboys have no interest in doing a deal until (Porter gets) on the field (to) see how good he is," the source said.
The Cowboys would be fine if they only had Porter as a one-year loaner for the remainder of this season, and Dallas is not believed to be planning to use the franchise tag on Porter or receiver George Pickens in 2027. However, that could change depending on how the two athletes play through the entirety of this season.

Per Pro Football Talk, if Dallas were to let Porter walk into free agency in 2027, the Cowboys would be set to receive a compensatory third-round pick in 2028 (closer to the start of the fourth round than the start of the third).
In a worst-case scenario where Porter does not agree to a new deal with Dallas, the Cowboys view the trade as giving up a second-round pick for a compensatory third while gaining one of the top coverage cornerbacks in the league this fall.
The Cowboys will enter the 2027 offseason with plenty of decisions to make about their roster. Dallas will have 20 players set to enter unrestricted free agency; six of those, including Porter and Pickens, are represented by David Mulugheta of Athletes First.
Dallas is in a better position to agree to a new deal with Porter than Pittsburgh. Per multiple reports , the heart of the dispute between Porter and the Steelers had to do with the guarantees in the deal. The Cowboys are more cash-rich than Pittsburgh and give more money guaranteed, more cash, and more signing bonus.
Another key factor that can help Porter is that the Cowboys, unlike the Steelers, have no state income taxes. Dallas can offer a higher signing bonus, which is not subject to state taxes. That will benefit Porter through the rest of this season as his game checks in Dallas won't be dinged for state taxes.

Boeing engineers and technical workers approved a sweetened four-year contract with immediate 10% raises, avoiding a potential strike at the aerospace giant as it seeks federal approval for new aircraft and to increase aircraft production.
"We secured many victories that some thought were completely out of reach when this negotiation cycle started," said the Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace, which represents about 13,000 Boeing engineers and 4,000 technical workers.
Boeing increased its offer in mid-September after the workers rejected an earlier proposal. In addition to the 10% ratification wage increase, the four-year contract includes annual raises of 4%, with an increase of up to 6% based on merit.
The professional unit, which includes engineers, voted 67.62% in favor of the new contract, and the tech unit approved the contract with 53.48% in favor, the union said.
The work groups, which make up Boeing's largest white-collar union, overwhelmingly rejected an earlier offer with 3% annual raises.
Boeing said in a statement that it was "pleased with the outcome of the vote."
The approval lets Boeing avoid a strike just as it's trying to stabilize and increase production of its fast-selling jets and win federal approval for the 737 Max 10 and 777X, which are years behind schedule.
The Federal Aviation Administration on Monday said it's assessing whether a software issue on the 737 Max 10, which could affect landing procedures in certain scenarios, poses a safety of flight issue.
A machinist strike two years ago halted production until the two sides reached a deal.

Bolivian police arrested the country’s top prosecutor and 13 others accused of protecting drug traffickers, the government said Thursday, days after the Trump administration imposed visa restrictions on the attorney general and several senior officials over corruption allegations.
The arrest of Bolivian Attorney General Roger Mariaca, appointed to a six-year term in 2024 under Bolivia’s previous socialist government, comes as conservative President Rodrigo Paz deepens security cooperation with Washington . U.S. Secretary State Marco Rubio hailed the arrests as “bold and decisive actions to combat narco-trafficking, systemic corruption, and transnational organized crime in Bolivia.”
Mariaca did not immediately comment on his arrest but had earlier denounced U.S. accusations that he accepted bribes to facilitate drug trafficking as political pressure on his office. Anti-drug prosecutor Miguel Gonzales said late Wednesday that police had detained Mariaca without a warrant.
“We have dismantled a criminal organization entrenched in the justice system,” Interior Minister Marco Antonio Oviedo told reporters Thursday, adding that Mariaca would face charges of money laundering and drug trafficking.
Authorities detained but swiftly released suspected Uruguayan drug kingpin Sebastián Marset in 2023, when Mariaca was chief prosecutor in the eastern region of Santa Cruz, Oviedo said. “They let him go, and not only that, they returned his seized assets,” he said of the longtime fugitive trafficker. Marset was ultimately captured in Bolivia last March and sent to the U.S. to face money laundering charges.
Oviedo also alleged that bundles of cash seized from an ambulance leaving Mariaca’s home in the city of Santa Cruz early Thursday were proceeds of extortion targeting people who sought help from prosecutors. Prosecutor Daniel Ortuño said officers found 3.53 million bolivianos (about $294,000) and an additional $10,000 in the vehicle.
The other detainees included two prosecutors also targeted by this week’s U.S. visa sanctions, part of a broader round of travel bans affecting over a dozen officials across South America.
The State Department cast Monday's measures as support for the Shield of the Americas, the Trump administration's security alliance with mostly conservative governments in the region, including Bolivia, to fight organized crime. The restrictions marked the latest instance of Washington using U.S. visas to pressure critics and officials whose actions conflict with its priorities in Latin America.
Urging lawmakers to overhaul the justice system, Oviedo warned officials against cooperating with criminal groups.
“Either you stand with the law ... or you stand with crime, with narcoterrorism,” he said.
Paz took office last November, ending nearly two decades of dominance by the Movement Toward Socialism party of former President Evo Morales . He has warmed ties with Washington and resumed cooperation with the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, which Morales expelled along with the U.S. ambassador in 2008, accusing them of seeking to overthrow his government.

House Democrats say officials may have illegally misused public funds to pay for president’s ‘narcissistic ego trips’
The Trump administration is facing growing questions over whether it illegally used taxpayer money to air television ads promoting Donald Trump five weeks before the US midterm elections .
Two congressional Democrats , Jamie Raskin of Maryland and George Whitesides of California, have asked federal watchdogs to investigate the ads.
Raskin, the top Democrat on the judiciary committee of the House of Representatives, and Whitesides wrote to the Government Accountability Office (GAO) and the office of special counsel (OSC) on Wednesday, describing the commercials as “desperate pre-election propaganda”.
The first ad was initially broadcast on 23 September. It shows dozens of images of Trump as a singer repeats “love me”, and the UFC president, Dana White, praises the president. A second ad, which aired days later, pairs footage of Trump with audio from a rally criticizing the “deep state”. Both end with fine print saying they were paid for by the US government.
“President Trump is obviously desperate for the American people to ‘love’ him, a problem that goes beyond your jurisdiction,” Raskin and Whitesides wrote in their letter. “But stealing taxpayer dollars to pay for Mr Trump’s narcissistic ego trips is plainly illegal.”
The lawmakers asked the GAO to identify the source and total amount of money used, and to issue a legal decision on whether the ads broke the law. They asked the OSC to investigate and determine who should be held accountable.
The lawmakers say the ads may violate four sets of laws , and cited a provision in this year’s spending act that bars funds for “publicity or propaganda”, along with the Anti-Deficiency Act, federal criminal statutes on misusing public money and the Hatch Act. The Hatch Act exempts the president but covers executive branch staff, and the lawmakers argue that employees must have helped produce the ads.
Raskin and Whitesides reject the White House’s description of the ads as public service announcements. They say nearly every claim in them is false, and that they are virtually identical to Trump’s 2024 campaign ads. In one example, they say an ad credits Trump with reviving manufacturing, though the US has lost tens of thousands of manufacturing jobs in his second term, according to a February report from Congress’s joint economic committee.
They also challenge the White House’s argument that the ads are not political because Trump is not on the ballot, though at an August rally he urged supporters to “pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot”.
A White House spokesperson has called the ads “educational and unapologetically patriotic”. Trump said on Wednesday that he would “gladly pay the money” if the ads were found to be improper.

Dana Walden joked at the beginning of her Bloomberg Screentime session Thursday that her job was to “keep this seat warm for Casey Bloys, who’s bringing the real news.”
Disney’s president and chief creative officer stuck to that promise when asked about the future of Jimmy Kimmel Live! Kimmel signed a one-year contract extension in December 2025 to keep hosting the late night show through the 2026-27 season, and Bloomberg’s Lucas Shaw asked Walden if the host would be sticking around.
“I’m not going to make that announcement here with you today,” Walden said. “Again, I’m letting Casey make the news.” (Bloys, the head of HBO and HBO Max, is the presumptive front-runner to head up streaming at the combined Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery when that megamerger closes in the coming days.)
Speculation about Jimmy Kimmel Live! ‘s future has swirled since an early September Page Six story claimed Kimmel’s contract wouldn’t be renewed. ABC quickly denied that was the case, but other reports said the network is looking for significant budget cuts to keep the show going.
“The truth is, it’s a very challenging daypart,” Walden said Thursday at the Bloomberg event. “That’s not to say that Jimmy is not doing a phenomenal job, and his ratings are up. But they’re up relative to a smaller audience that’s watching late night on broadcast television.”
Kimmel and the show also have a big presence on YouTube and social media platforms, but those views and clicks bring in a fraction of the revenue that on-air advertising does. “That is not a lucrative opportunity for a very premium talk show,” said Walden.
“We’re trying to make sense of the business while also honoring a deep partnership,” she continued. “I love Jimmy; we have great friendship. He’s close to a number of the people at Disney. We’re trying to work through it and make sense of, what does Jimmy want, what’s the right thing to do, and what’s the right thing for our business.”

articles.title_orig: Judge permanently ends case against Olympian accused of Reflecting Pool vandalism
articles.title_zh: Judge permanently ends case against Olympian accused of Reflecting Pool vandalism
articles.content_orig:
A judge in Washington DC has dismissed the criminal case against an Olympian accused by the Trump administration of vandalising the Reflecting Pool.
Judge Todd Edelman ordered the case against David Hearn dismissed "with prejudice", meaning US prosecutors cannot refile the case.
The US Justice Department had dropped the case after new evidence emerged, but Hearn's lawyers expressed concern that US President Donald Trump could pressure prosecutors to revive it.
Issues with the pool were the result of a "rushed and botched" job by contractors, the government found, but Trump has repeatedly claimed it was due to vandalism and urged prosecutors to target Hearn, citing donations to Democrats.
The cases against three other people also accused of vandalising the pool were dropped as well, but Hearn's defence attorneys said they were worried he would be specifically targeted by Trump because he is a politically active person who previously made campaign donations to Democrats.
In permanently dismissing the case, Edelman agreed with those concerns and pointed to public statements made by Trump after his chief prosecutor for the District of Columbia, Jeanine Pirro, dropped the case.
"Although the prosecutors assigned to this case have deemed it meritless, the president of the United States has repeatedly disparaged them and pressured them to change course," the judge said in his order, published on Thursday.
"Mr Hearn faces the unique possibility that the government will revive this case – one that it has already announced to be meritless – based on political pressure brought by the president of the United States upon his subordinate officers."
Hearn, a champion canoeist, had been facing a 10-year prison sentence if he had been found guilty. He previously told the BBC that he was riding his bike near the pool when he reached down to touch a piece of the lining that was peeling.
The Justice Department said new information from the Department of Interior (DOI) indicated "that damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in June 2026 was the result of flawed installation by the contractor" and "the rush to complete the project prior to events associated with the America 250 celebration in the weeks surrounding Independence Day 2026".
The concession represented a stunning about-face for prosecutors who had just days before accused Hearn of "a deliberate act to damage the Reflecting Pool".
Trump then took to social media to say he disagreed "100%" with Pirro's decision to drop the charges, describing it in separate statements as "a disgrace" and "stupid".
"There may have been some contractor difficulty, but the major damage was caused by VANDALS!" the president wrote in August. Trump has urged Pirro to revive the case against Hearn.
"US Attorney Jeanine Pirro should re-visit her hastily made decision, especially since it turned out that the 'gentleman' involved is a big player in ActBlue," he said on 7 August, referring to Hearn and the campaign fundraising platform used by Democrats.
He also disparaged Norm Eisen, one of the attorneys representing Hearn, who previously worked for President Barack Obama, as well as on an impeachment case against Trump during his first term.
Hearn's legal team hailed the permanent dismissal as "a victory for the rule of law".
"This administration chose to pursue an unjust prosecution against Mr. Hearn. It should not get repeated chances to wield the power of criminal prosecution against someone who should never have been prosecuted," they said. "Today's decision protects Mr. Hearn from that threat, allowing him to move forward with his life as he deserves."
Asked for comment about the decision, a White House spokesperson referred the BBC to Trump's online comments which were cited by the judge, including his suggestion the case should not have been dropped. The BBC has also contacted Pirro's office and the justice department for comment.
The Lincoln Memorial and the adjoining Reflecting Pool have been the site of many landmark events including civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr's famous "I have a dream" speech.
It underwent a multi-million dollar resealing and painting project this spring, one of several construction efforts in the US capital personally directed by Trump.
The monument had long been beset by structural failures and leaks, and Trump championed the project as part of his bid to beautify the capital city.
But, despite the makeover, which cost an estimated $16m (£12m), the pool continued to be plagued by algae, while pieces of the blue sealant peeled off days after it was applied.

articles.title_orig: As Mortgage Rates Hit Highest Level Since 2023, Buyers Look at ARMs
articles.title_zh: As Mortgage Rates Hit Highest Level Since 2023, Buyers Look at ARMs
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates keep going up.
The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.28% this week, up from 7.03% last week, according to Freddie Mac data released Thursday. Mortgage rates have risen for six straight weeks, and this week brought the biggest one-week jump in nearly four years. Rates are now at their highest level since November 2023.
Turmoil in the bond market is driving rates higher. The 10-year Treasury yield has risen in recent months as investors worry that the Iran war and increased government spending could further stoke inflation and push the Federal Reserve toward higher rates for longer.
If you’re currently in the market for a home, the good news is you may be facing less competition from rate-sensitive buyers who are stepping back. But if you need a mortgage, the bad news is you will likely pay more in monthly costs than you would have just a few months ago.
But even with borrowing costs high – and potentially headed higher – a sub-7% mortgage rate may still be within reach for some buyers. The trade-off could be a riskier loan or a much bigger upfront payment.
Most home buyers opt for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage because it typically offers lower monthly payments and predictable costs.
But it’s not the only option. Other types of mortgages may offer lower interest rates, potentially saving borrowers money over the life of the loan.
A 15-year mortgage typically has a lower interest rate than a 30-year mortgage, though monthly payments are significantly higher. Another option that is becoming increasingly popular lately: adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs).
As of the latest data last week, “ARM loans, with rates around 80 basis points lower than fixed rate loans, accounted for 10.3% of applications, the highest share since October 2025,” according to Joel Kan, deputy chief economist at the Mortgage Bankers Association.
How are higher interest rates and rising prices affecting you?
But ARM loans, the mortgage products that helped fuel housing market risk in the lead-up to the 2008 financial crisis, are riskier than fixed-rate loans . They typically offer a lower fixed rate for five, seven or 10 years before resetting with market rates. If rates are higher when the fixed period ends, borrowers can be hit with sharply higher monthly payments.
“It may work well for some borrowers who are expecting to move or refinance in four or five years,” said Jeremy Luke, a divisional director at Chase Home Lending. “It may not work for all.”
Another way to get a lower mortgage rate is to take over someone’s existing mortgage as an assumable loan .
Not all home loans can be passed to a home buyer, but most government-backed loans, such as those from the Federal Housing Administration, the US Department of Veterans Affairs and the US Department of Agriculture, are assumable.
However, the approval process for an assumable mortgage can take longer. And because the buyer takes over only the seller’s remaining loan balance, they may need to bring significantly more cash to the table to cover the difference between that balance and the home’s purchase price.
The rate an individual buyer gets depends on more than market conditions. Lenders also consider factors such as the borrower’s credit score, debt-to-income ratio and down payment, said Jeff DerGurahian, head economist at loanDepot.
After shopping around, if you are unsatisfied with the rates you’ve been offered, it’s often possible to pay more up front in exchange for a reduced interest rate.
Permanent buydowns lower your interest rate for the life of the loan, whereas temporary buydowns, which can be cheaper, lower your rate for only the first few years.
But it’s important not to overdo it, DerGurahian said.
“You don’t want to put so much money down that you can’t do what you need to do to live in your house and live day-to-day,” he said.
Sometimes, the home’s seller or a builder can cover the cost of a rate buydown.
Builders are leaning more heavily on incentives to attract buyers to new construction, offering concessions such as mortgage rate buydowns and closing-cost credits. In September, 66% of builders reported using sales incentives, up from 63% in August and the highest share since December, according to the National Association of Home Builders’ sentiment survey.
A buyer should also understand the demand picture in their local market, said DerGurahian.
If it’s a buyer’s market, that means the supply of homes in that area exceeds demand, giving home buyers the upper hand. If a homeowner is motivated to sell, they may be willing to offer concessions to attract a buyer. If sellers have the upper hand in a local market, though, it’s less likely.
Certain buyers may have access to federal programs that can help them secure more favorable mortgage rates, including VA loans for eligible veterans and USDA loans for buyers purchasing homes in qualifying rural areas.
There are also banks and credit unions that offer relationship pricing or preferential rates.
For example, Chase occasionally runs “rate sales” where home buyers (and homeowners looking to refinance) can lock in discounted rates, Luke said.
Some banks, including Chase, also offer a discounted rate if customers move eligible deposits and investments into that bank, Luke added.
It pays to shop around. Experts generally recommend applying with at least three different mortgage lenders to make sure you’re getting a competitive rate. Compare the rates offered, closing costs and other fees to get a clearer picture of the total cost of each loan.
And you don’t necessarily have to worry about multiple credit checks dinging your score. To shop around for mortgages without hurting your credit, limit your search to a window of 14 to 45 days, according to Bankrate.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Friendly-faced California tech CEO arrested by feds for allegedly hiding $300M Chinese secret
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Friendly-faced California tech CEO arrested by feds for allegedly hiding $300M Chinese secret
articles.content_orig:
Federal agents on Wednesday arrested a California tech CEO who’s accused of smuggling more than $300 million in restricted AI chips into China.
Greg Lui, 38, aka “Yiu Kong Lui,” of San Gabriel, faces a barrage of federal charges for allegedly selling Beijing a mountain of American-made AI graphics processors in violation of US laws, potentially threatening national security.
The California Post watched as the FBI and Department of Commerce agents arrested the high-flying tech boss in a stealth raid at the City of Industry headquarters of Earthmade Computers, a company Lui founded and runs, and which he allegedly used to conduct the profitable yet illegal scheme.
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
Agents tracked Lui as he drove a Tesla Cybertruck with a white wrap from his gigantic San Gabriel mansion to the Earthmade’s shiny offices in a tidy industrial park, handcuffing him at gunpoint soon after he arrived at work. Lui didn’t speak as he was placed in a vehicle to be taken in for processing.
AI is now used in nearly every aspect of modern warfare, and investigators said the advanced tech allegedly smuggled by Lui could’ve easily been put to use by the Chinese military.
“Protecting America’s national security means keeping our advanced Super Intelligence technology from being used to strengthen our adversaries’ military capabilities,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli.
“This defendant allegedly used false paperwork and shipments through third countries to smuggle more than $300 million in export-controlled computer servers to China,” Essayli added. We will aggressively prosecute those who put our national security at risk for profit.”
Federal prosecutors say Lui and his co-conspirators used Earthmade to buy and send sensitive AI tech into China from 2023 to 2024, without the required licenses issued by DOC that are meant to promote US foreign policy and protect national security.
Instead, they shipped these items to countries such as Malaysia and Singapore, where no licenses are required, and then illegally re-exported them to China.
The items in question were high-end computer servers, containing processors made by Nvidia Corp , a Santa Clara tech company specializing in AI. According to federal regulations, such tech could make significant contributions to Chinese armed forces.
As part of the alleged scheme, prosecutors say, Lui and his conspirators used fake documents to show the potentially dangerous AI tech would be going to destinations that did not require an export license in orders they placed with suppliers such as Nvidia.
After making these orders, Lui hired freight forwarding companies to ship the processors to Malaysia and Singapore . Once the servers arrived in these locations, Lui worked with his conspirators to reship the items to China.
From January 2024 to October 2024, Earthmade received more than $176 million from two Malaysia-based shipment companies as part of the scheme, according to court papers.
Prosecutors say Lui executed the scam knowing what he did was illegal, and they have the evidence to prove it.
For example, prosecutors say, Lui emailed a conspirator in January 2024 saying a Malaysian transshipment company wanted to buy 70 computer servers with the controlled AI tech. In the email, he noted the laws against the sale of such tech, according to court papers.
Later that month Lui purchased 27 of the servers for roughly $7.6 million and sent the servers from LA to Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Two months later, one of Lui’s conspirators told a Malaysian official in an email that the servers had, in fact, been transshipped to China.
Prosecutors say Lui used a LA-based JP Morgan Chase account and Bank of America account to send and receive money to orchestrate the scheme.
Lui is charged with one count of conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act , one count of smuggling and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. If convicted he faces up to 50 years in prison.
Before his arrest Lui lived a luxurious lifestyle, recently completing an extensive renovation of the 4,300-square foot mansion on Walnut Grove Avenue that he used to house numerous members of his extended family.
Federal agents were seen conducting a search of the massive spread Thursday, recording video and carrying evidence from the nine-bedroom, seven-bathroom home that has two stories and just got new stucco and windows, a fresh driveway and other upgrades.
The US DOC, the Defense Criminal Investigative Service and the FBI are investigating the case.
According to his LinkedIn page, Lui has an eight-year career in tech that began with a stint at Amplitude Tech Hosting Service, a Denver-based firm specializing in database colocation.
In 2021 he founded Earthmade Computer, which also handles database colocation, in addition to computer processor procurement and export, according to LinkedIn.
Before his tech run, Lui was a restauranter who specialized in ultra-spicy Sichuan Chinese food. In 2012 he co-founded of Duo-Pot in Arcadia, a Chinese hot pot and dry pot joint that sold spicy frog dishes before it closed in 2021, according to LinkedIn.

Force” — captured an American president operating unpredictably across multiple fronts even as each one drew friction. The actions now stand to color the backdrop of a week that will feature meetings with world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly in New York and a state visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.
Each of those moves carries its own political weight ahead of the diplomatic talks, but also ahead of the midterm elections, where these topics are front and center in key races.
Trump’s handling of the Iran war, its subsequent shocks to the global economy, his push to fast-track the development of artificial intelligence and the Greenland agreement are likely to come up in meetings with world leaders. His deal with Denmark to bolster U.S. military presence in Greenland, a territory Trump has repeatedly tried to annex , is expected to be signed  Tuesday in New York, though action is still needed by the Danish and Greenland governments before it can be enforced.
While all the details of the Greenland deal are not public yet, Trump has said it is a “dream come true for the United States of America.”

In an interview  Sunday, Trump also indicated that he was trying to make a decision on Iran as the war stretches into its eighth month. The president said he would “probably be open” to meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian during the U.N. General Assembly.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico will challenge the constitutionality of President Trump’s order to ban the news organizations from the White House.
Of all the actions Trump took, the press dispute has become the most contentious and drawn an immediate legal response. Three major news outlets — CNN, MS NOW and Politico — sued the Trump administration Monday for banning their reporters from the White House grounds, and major television networks suspended their pool coverage of the president’s activities.
In a joint statement, the organizations said the White House has acted “without notice or process” and called the arbitrary decision a “blatant violation” of the 1st Amendment.
Trump, meanwhile, argued  Monday that the banned  news outlets  are “corrupt” and a “threat to our national security.”
Vice President JD Vance defended the press ban.
“He’s not banning media outlets. What he’s doing is saying we’re not going to give you special access to the White House if you engage in what is effectively propaganda,” Vance said Monday, arguing that the three outlets push out “negative” coverage of Trump.
The tense showdown between Trump and the White House press corps led to audio problems during the president’s ribbon-cutting ceremony for a new helipad on the South Lawn. Without television cameras and microphones set up by the major TV networks, it was impossible to hear what  Trump was saying through the White House’s official YouTube stream, signaling  further technical difficulties in the week ahead.
Behind the public displays of control, news reports have painted a picture of a president increasingly frustrated by the lack of credit he feels he is owed. At a recent closed-door meeting, reported by the Wall Street Journal , Trump told advisors he was aggravated that his allies hadn’t lauded him enough for his efforts to take over the Kennedy Center or other accomplishments made during his second term.
Trump has tried to put his name on the building’s facade and run into resistance from Democrats, arts patrons and a federal judge who blocked the move last week. Trump was then photographed aboard Air Force One looking at a large printout appearing to show demolition plans for the center.

Trump’s announcement over the weekend comes as lawmakers, including congressional Republicans in tight  races, have called for new guardrails on the technology.

Sony is launching a new AI upscaling technology specifically for the regular PS5. The new tech, called Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR), is a “new performance tier of AI upscaling” that’s a result of Sony’s Project Amethyst work with AMD, according to a blog post .
Sony says that PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR), which is available on the PS5 Pro , “remains the gold standard,” and in Digital Foundry ’s early hands-on with the tech , it does seem that QSSR isn’t as fast as PSSR because the PS5 doesn’t have dedicated machine learning silicon. As a result, you should probably expect closer to an upscaled 1440p resolution on PS5 instead of the upscaled 4K on PS5 Pro.
”On PS5 Pro, developers almost uniformly output to 4K and adjust render resolution beneath it,” Sony principal graphics R&D engineer Daniel Craig told Digital Foundry . “On PS5, teams have to be more flexible, tuning not just render resolution, but also their intermediate and final presentation targets depending on the graphics mode.”
But Craig also said that QSSR is “fundamentally a drop-in replacement for titles that already support PSSR” after only a few days of tuning, making it likelier that PS5 developers will take advantage. The tech will be “offered broadly to all PlayStation developers,” Sony says.
Marvel’s Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei will be the first games to take advantage of QSSR, and are getting patches today to offer the tech as “an additional graphics option on PS5.” ( Ghost of Yōtei Complete Edition also launches today .) Here are a couple videos from Sony showing off how QSSR looks in those games, and it appears to make graphics a little bit sharper:
Digital Foundry writes that “the potential here is remarkable: low resolution and poor upscaling have impacted so many titles in this generation, but QSSR could make a big difference.”

articles.title_orig: Cornell Jane Doe's attorney says she told police in 2024: 'I was raped'
articles.title_zh: Cornell Jane Doe's attorney says she told police in 2024: 'I was raped'
articles.content_orig:
Students walk on the campus of Cornell University on Wednesday in Ithaca, N.Y. Spencer Platt/Getty Images hide caption
The woman who alleges she was gang raped by fellow Cornell University students in 2024 clearly stated in her statement to police two years ago that she was sexually assaulted.
That's according to her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, who confirmed to NPR that his client told investigators, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped," citing transcripts from Jane Doe's sworn statement in 2024.
NPR asked Giuffra to specifically confirm on the record to NPR that his client made this exact quoted statement regarding her assault. His response by text: "Yes she did."
This is in contrast to statements from the local prosecutor, who claimed on Monday that Doe never stated she was raped. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten told NPR local station WSKG on Wednesday that he had not read the full account of her detailed statements to investigators where she repeatedly described being assaulted.
NPR asked Cornell if campus police provided the DA with all of the information from their investigation, including her repeated statements about being assaulted. The university did not respond to the request for comment.
CBS News New York reported Wednesday on a transcript of an interview between the Cornell University Police Department investigator and the alleged victim. NPR has not been able to obtain a copy of these transcripts.
Van Houten said in Monday's statement that in the 2024 statement taken by Cornell University police, Doe "did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual."
No criminal charges were ever filed against the seven men Doe alleges drugged and assaulted her for several hours in October 2024.
Van Houten told NPR member station WSKG on Wednesday evening that he was in the process of getting the interview transcript from Cornell. He told the station over email that he doesn't know when he will get the transcript from the university "or if Cornell will resist turning it over."
"If it's factual, we absolutely should have been informed about what Jane Doe said to police that was not in her six-page statement," he told WSKG.
Van Houten said earlier this week that his office is reexamining the case.
He added that particular transcript is part of the confidential Title IX investigation Cornell launched into the alleged assault.
In mid-September, Doe filed a lawsuit against the seven men who she alleges assaulted her two years ago. Cornell was also named in the lawsuit.
Following the onslaught of public backlash against Cornell and the local prosecutor, the school said Wednesday night that it will bring in an outside counsel to conduct an independent probe into the handling of the case.
Since Tuesday, Cornell has directed the public to an FAQ page on the rape allegations.
The university has maintained that Cornell University Police investigated the case thoroughly and that the school held its own Title IX investigation, which resulted in suspensions and expulsions. Cornell has not specified how many students faced punishments, or of what nature. It noted in the FAQ: "Federal privacy law prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individual students, and the university is therefore unable to make a public statement regarding any other disciplinary response."
WSKG found that as of Wednesday, the university has changed its FAQ. And it has quietly removed a sentence stating that the Cornell police "shared all investigatory information with the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office."
Previously, the FAQ read: "The Cornell University Police Department investigated the matter in 2024 and shared all investigatory information with the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office, which is the established protocol if the department believes it is possible a crime has occurred."
But by Wednesday afternoon , WSKG found that statement had been edited, and any mention of Cornell police sharing "all investigatory information" with the district attorney had disappeared from the page.
"The Cornell University Police Department is a unit of the university, and its officers are sworn Tompkins County deputy sheriffs whose duties include the enforcement of law and order on Cornell property," the new statement reads. "This incident occurred in Cornell's jurisdiction."
WSKG reported that Cornell University did not respond to its questions about these changes.
Students at the university have expressed outrage and deep disappointment toward school officials for their handling of this case. The Cornell University Student Assembly scheduled a public hearing set for Thursday afternoon during which they say they will "demand institutional accountability" from their school.
"We stand unequivocally with survivors of sexual violence, and we remain committed to ensuring that their voices are not only heard, but met with action," the organization said in a statement on Instagram .
Late Wednesday, the school confirmed to NPR that it is bringing in an outside counsel to hold an independent examination of the alleged gang rape.
University officials told NPR they have no further details about how the investigation will play out. Previously, Cornell strongly defended how it handled the case when Doe first reported the incident to school officials two years ago.
The move comes after New York Gov. Kathy Hochul called for the school to open an outside investigation. In a video posted on X , Hochul also said she's considering new legislation to tighten sexual assault laws across the state.
"While we have some of the toughest laws on sexual assault on college campuses right here in New York, I think we can do better," she said. "This culture has to stop. And it will stop here in the state of New York."
WSKG's Aurora Berry contributed reporting.
